summary:
Afghanistan is the most hostile jurisdiction on this map for a transgender visitor. The EUAA COI Report of February 2026 records that no legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity existed before the 2021 takeover and none exists after it. The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024, in Article 22, obliges the regime's overseers to prevent listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality "even if with one's own spouse", placing same-sex conduct under continuous moral surveillance alongside adultery and gambling.

Criminalisation is layered. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, records that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on "sodomy" and "inciting sodomy" carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity. Per Amnesty International, as cited in the EUAA COI Report, same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Enforcement is visible and escalating. An OHCHR press release of March 2026 reports that UN human-rights experts condemned the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment, with at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warned that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for "moral crimes" including adultery, "illicit relationships" and "sodomy". OutRight International reported in February 2023, from 22 interviews conducted in September and October 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country, that Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in the early months of rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; punishments the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed on social media. CNN reported in November 2024 first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody as the crackdown intensified.

The Human Rights Watch and OutRight report of 26 January 2022, 43 pages based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans, found that Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes, that abuse by family, neighbours and partners surged after the takeover, and that many went into hiding or fled. A DW feature of 2 October 2021 profiles trans people hiding in Kabul and documents street attacks on men coded as gay, who changed their clothing and confined themselves indoors. The JURIST feature of 8 November 2024, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen, reports systematic persecution after August 2021 and states that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks, including exploitation and violence.

Marriage and partnership recognition do not exist. Under Taliban rule post-2021, same-sex relationships and marriages are not recognised at all. Under the Islamic Republic the 1971 Law of Marriages required a legal marriage to be between two Muslim adults of the opposite sex, with Article 41 directing that gaps be resolved by Islamic law principles, and the 1949 Law on Marriages, Weddings and Circumcision likewise framed marriage as between a Muslim man and woman, so no same-sex marriage, civil union or domestic partnership was recognised in either period.

Two protection mechanisms are documented. The EUAA Country Guidance of May 2024, section 3.17, treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious and social norms alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty, and this framing is the asylum-assessment basis for Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU. On 23 January 2025 the ICC Prosecutor requested arrest warrants against Taliban leaders Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani for persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ community, the first time the court has recognised crimes against the LGBTQ community.
tangentialFactors:
The legal architecture predating 2021 was already restrictive. Article 430 of the criminal code made it an "Instigation of Delinquency" for an adult to promote or assist a minor in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution, a provision capable of reaching any adult including a caregiver or partner, and Article 427 increased punishment where the victim was under 18. Article 398 offered lesser punishment for vigilante honour killings that can target minors found engaging in homosexuality, and Article 373 imposed fines or murder-equivalent penalties for spreading a "dangerous disease". Persons convicted of homosexuality were generally sentenced to prison in the cities under the Islamic Republic.

No law addressed discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity under the republic, and political parties were prohibited from advocating anything opposing Islamic morality. The 2017 U.S. State Department report found that LGBTI community members did not have access to certain health services and could be fired from jobs because of sexual orientation, and that organisations protecting LGBTI freedom remained underground because they could not legally register with the government; the 2020 report confirmed that status.

Information about sexual orientation and gender identity has been constrained by censorship as well as infrastructure. The 2002 Press Law, Article 32, prohibits "incitement to depravity" and Article 27(D) of the 1973 Postal Law bars material "repugnant to public decency"; Hamid Zaher's 2009 memoir about growing up gay in Afghanistan, It Is Your Enemy Who Is Dock-Tailed, cannot be distributed within the country. A 2011 survey found young men displaying rainbow symbols unaware of their meaning and quickly removing them, and the 2017 and 2020 State Department reports noted that awareness of sexual orientation or gender identity remained limited and that homosexuality was widely seen as taboo.

Accounts from outside the country frame the situation in starkly similar terms across sources. The JURIST feature notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework for LGBT Afghans. The DW feature of October 2021 states that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and that their only option is to leave, a formulation that matches the flight and hiding described in the Human Rights Watch and OutRight interviews of January 2022 and the in-country interviews of OutRight's February 2023 report.
localsOnly:
Care access is constrained by law, stigma and limited infrastructure. Before 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; the 2008 official count was 504 people living with HIV-AIDS, though the true figure was suspected to be in the thousands. The first HIV-AIDS treatment centre opened in Kabul in 2009 with more clinics promised, access to anti-retroviral drugs is at best limited, and the 2020 State Department report states that the government only permits condom distribution to married couples, excluding same-sex couples, while noting stigma against people living with HIV. Low literacy, weak infrastructure and social taboos impede comprehensive public health education.

Youth are a documented target. Bacha bazi involves teenage boys kidnapped, dressed in women's clothing, made to dance in competitions and forced into sexual acts; militia members without access to women kidnap boys to be humiliated and raped, other boys become prostitutes regardless of sexual orientation, and the practice was prevalent in big cities and reported in 2007 as still common in northern Afghanistan. US-backed Northern Alliance warlords kidnapped, trafficked and raped young boys after 2001, yet neither the U.S. Department of Defense nor the Afghan government acted despite awareness. President Hamid Karzai signed an agreement to ban the practice and a law prohibited Afghan soldiers from having their "ashna" ("friend") live with them, but it was rarely enforced and police were reportedly complicit.

When the Taliban came to power in 1996 they banned bacha bazi alongside homosexuality, both carrying the death penalty, and under the Islamic Republic young victims were often charged rather than the adult perpetrators. Article 430 can deter adults from seeking care for minors by treating any adult who promotes or assists minors in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution as committing "Instigation of Delinquency".

Article 430 of the criminal code reaches adults in same-sex households directly as well: a caregiver or partner involved with a same-sex partner or family can be charged under it, and Article 427 aggravates the offence where the victim is under 18. The 2017 and 2020 State Department reports record that LGBTI people could be dismissed from employment on grounds of sexual orientation and that LGBTI advocacy organisations could not legally register.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry and visa rules, passport or gender-marker documentation, airport screening, or facilities access for transgender visitors; those layers of the profile remain unsourced rather than confirmed absent.

Two readings of the penalty exposure sit side by side in the sources and are not reconciled: the Penal Code 2017 provisions cited by the Human Dignity Trust carry a maximum of two years' imprisonment, while the code's Sharia-reference clause and Amnesty International's characterisation point to the death penalty. Which penalty applies in practice for a given charge under the current authorities is unresolved in the material available.

The inventory does not document whether the death penalty has in fact been carried out since 2021 for same-sex conduct specifically. The March 2026 OHCHR figures cover public flogging across 2025 without breaking out how many cases involved alleged sodomy or other same-sex conduct.

Hate-crime protection, non-discrimination enforcement and any complaint or redress machinery for visitors are not sourced for the current period; the closest material concerns the pre-2021 absence of such law and the pending ICC warrant requests, which are not a visitor-facing remedy.
